title: Honor
hookLine: honoring others, and not chasing honor

lines: WHO IS WISE? WHO IS STRONG?
cards: Who is wise? Who is strong? Who is rich?

Who is honored? Ben Zoma asks these in the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, and each answer flips the one you'd expect. The wise person isn't the one with a wall of diplomas; it's the one who learns from everyone.
The strong one isn't the winner of fights; it's the one who masters their own impulse. The rich one is happy with their portion. And the honored one?
Ben Zoma's last answer turns honor around completely.

teach.h: WHO IS HONORED? WHO HONORS OTHERS.
teach.b: Kavod. Honor. Turn it four ways.
First, Ben Zoma's answer: the honored person is the one who honors others. Honor isn't a trophy you collect. It's something you hand out, and it ends up describing the giver.
In Hebrew, kavod is built on the same three letters as kaved, heavy. The Torah's command to honor your father and mother uses those letters too.
To honor someone is to treat them as weighty: their words count, their time counts, their being in the room counts. Third, the chase.
The Talmud, in tractate Eruvin, says that whoever chases greatness, greatness runs away from them, and whoever runs from greatness, greatness follows.
On the same page it asks why the law follows the school of Hillel over the school of Shammai.
Its answer: Hillel's students were gentle and humble, and they taught Shammai's words alongside their own, even putting Shammai's first. They gave honor, and it came back to them. Fourth, the proof.

teach.h: THOSE WHO HONOR ME, I WILL HONOR.
teach.b: Ben Zoma backs his answer with a verse from Samuel, where God says, in effect: those who honor me, I will honor.

If honor comes back even to those who honor God, he reasons, it belongs all the more between people. Like yesterday's chesed, honor gives past what the other person can demand, and leaves the giver larger, not smaller.

how: Jewish practice builds honor into daily life: standing for elders and teachers, honoring parents, and in Mussar groups, working on kavod by noticing when one seeks credit and choosing to give it instead.

o: pride in your own good name

p: who is honored? who honors others

s: Ben Zoma says the honored person is the one with the highest position
he says the honored one is the one who honors others.
kavod and the word for heavy are spelled with the same letters
to honor someone is to treat them as weighty.
the Talmud says the law follows Hillel because his school was larger
it says Hillel's students were gentle and humble, and taught Shammai's words first.

games.q: two schools have argued for years. the law will follow one of them. why does the Talmud say it follows Hillel's school?
o: they were gentle and humble, and taught the other school's words first.
games.why: Eruvin says Hillel's students were gentle and humble and taught Shammai's words, even before their own. they gave honor, and it came back.

practice: Bring to mind someone close whose worth you've stopped saying out loud: a parent, a sibling, a colleague whose idea you once took credit for.

Find one specific thing they do well, something real, and shape it into a sentence you could say to them, or about them where it would reach them. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer by name.

wordCard.voice: Kavod. Honor: treating others as weighty, given rather than chased. Who is honored? The one who honors others. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: give honor. The one who honors others is the one honored. One more day up the hill.
